> 中孚。豚魚吉，利涉大川，利貞。

Hexagram 61 is about trust, and its character is a bird sitting on an egg.

## 孚 is 卵孚 — hatching

說文: 孚，卵孚也. Built from 爪 over 子 — a claw over a child.

So the original sense is to brood, to hatch. "Trust" is the extension.

Which is the most important layer in this chapter. 孚 means sitting still on something until, in its own time, it turns into a bird.

So trust in the 易 is never "we agreed." It is keeping something warm. Give it no time and it will not hatch; turn it over every day and it dies.

中孚: the thing inside that is being hatched.

## 虞 and 它

虞: originally a beast's name (騶虞), borrowed for "to reckon," "to prepare." 虞吉 — measure first, guard first.

它: originally a snake (the old form of 它 is the snake pictograph), borrowed for "other." 有它不燕 — if something else is in the heart, there is no rest.

Read as "other," and the line is exactly right: a snake has entered the house, and the person cannot settle.

So the first line of 中孚 is not about sincerity at all. It is about the second thing: the whole hexagram requires that there be only one animal in the room.

## 鳴鶴在陰，其子和之

Nine-two is the most quoted verse in the book:

> 鳴鶴在陰，其子和之；我有好爵，吾與爾靡之.

A crane calls in the shade, and its young answers. I have a fine cup, and I share it with you.

靡 here is "together with," "to share out."

Which is the hexagram's positive image of trust: not an oath, an answer. One voice, and a second voice coming back from the same shade — that is what 孚 looks like when it is working.

## 得敵，或鼓或罷，或泣或歌

Six-three: meeting a match — now drumming, now stopping; now weeping, now singing.

Four alternatives in one line, and none of them is a decision. Which is the exact opposite of hatching: this is a thing being turned over constantly, and the line has no verdict because the situation has none.

## 月幾望，馬匹亡

Six-four: the moon nearly full; the team of horses is lost; no fault.

匹 is a pair, a matched team. Losing the pair at the point of near-fullness.

Set against 小畜上九 and 歸妹六五, which also carry 月幾望: the same phase of the moon, three different verdicts. Here it is 无咎 — because what was given up was the pair, and the fullness is not one's own.

## 有孚攣如

九五: 有孚攣如，無咎.

攣: to bind (說文 攣，系也).

Trust like a rope, binding people into one place.

Not "trust like a feeling." A line that holds. Which is the strongest statement 中孚 makes, and it is in the ruler's seat.

## 翰音

Top line: 有孚攣如… 翰音登于天，貞凶.

翰 is the heavenly cock; and 翰音 is the ritual name of the chicken — 禮記·曲禮: 雞曰翰音, sacrifice avoids saying "chicken" and names its voice instead.

(One draft of this book read it as "the cry of a flying bird." That is reading the words and missing the referent. 翰音 is a chicken.)

So the last line is: a chicken, crowing loud enough to reach heaven, still standing at the foot of the wall.

Which is the chapter's closing danger, and it is not insincerity. It is the sound of trust without the body of it — a voice at full volume with nothing underneath.

## 議獄緩死

The 象: 君子以議獄緩死 — review the case, and slow the death.

議: to weigh the offence. 緩: to loosen.

A hexagram about hatching ends at the place where the state must be most careful with time: the sentence that cannot be taken back.

## The test

Take something you are waiting on — a relationship, a piece of work, a decision that has not ripened. Ask the 孚 question: are you brooding it or turning it over? And the top line's: is there a body under the crowing?
